facts.title: Born in a German Lab
facts.text: Copernicium was first created on February 9, 1996, at the GSI Helmholtz Centre for Heavy Ion Research in Darmstadt, Germany. A team led by Sigurd Hofmann fired zinc-70 ions at a lead-208 target, fusing two nuclei to make a single atom of element 112. It took years more of careful experiments and independent confirmation before the discovery was officially accepted in 2009.

facts.title: Named for an Astronomer
facts.text: The element honors Nicolaus Copernicus, the Renaissance scholar who placed the Sun, not the Earth, at the center of the solar system. The name was proposed by the GSI discovery team and made official by IUPAC on February 19, 2010, the 537th anniversary of Copernicus's birth. It is one of the few elements named after a person who was not himself a chemist or physicist.

facts.title: Gone in an Instant
facts.text: Copernicium is intensely radioactive and decays almost as soon as it forms. Its most stable known isotope, copernicium-285, has a half-life of roughly 28 to 30 seconds, while many other isotopes survive for only milliseconds. This fleeting existence is why scientists have only ever made a handful of atoms at a time.

facts.title: A Superheavy Heavyweight
facts.text: With 112 protons packed into its nucleus, copernicium sits deep in the realm of "superheavy" elements. Atoms this large are held together against enormous electrical repulsion, and they exist near the predicted "island of stability" where certain proton and neutron counts may grant longer lifetimes. Studying them tests the very limits of how big an atom can be.

facts.title: Maybe a Liquid Metal
facts.text: Copernicium sits below mercury in the periodic table, and theory predicts it could be a volatile metal, possibly even a gas or liquid at room temperature. The reason is Einstein's relativity: electrons in such a heavy atom move at a large fraction of light speed, which contracts their orbitals and weakens the metallic bonding. This would make copernicium behave more like a noble gas than a typical transition metal.

facts.title: Tested Atom by Atom
facts.text: Because only single atoms can be made, chemists study copernicium using a technique called gas-phase chromatography, watching where one atom sticks to a gold-coated surface. In 2006 and later experiments, researchers compared how copernicium and mercury atoms deposited on cold detectors. The results hinted that copernicium is indeed more volatile and less metallic than mercury, just as relativity predicts.

facts.title: Not Found in Nature
facts.text: Copernicium does not occur naturally anywhere on Earth, in meteorites, or in the stars we can observe. Every atom that has ever existed was deliberately manufactured in a particle accelerator. Because its isotopes decay so quickly, even if it once formed in a cosmic explosion, none could have survived to the present day.

facts.title: A Stepping Stone in Decay Chains
facts.text: Copernicium often appears not as a target but as a product, born when heavier elements decay. Isotopes of flerovium (element 114), for example, shed an alpha particle and transform into copernicium on their way down to lighter atoms. Tracking these alpha-decay chains is exactly how scientists confirm that a new superheavy element was really created.

facts.title: From Placeholder to Real Name
facts.text: Before it had a permanent name, element 112 was called ununbium, a Latin-Greek placeholder literally meaning "one-one-two." IUPAC uses such systematic names for any element that has been claimed but not yet officially confirmed and named. Copernicium's journey from "ununbium" to a proper name shows how rigorously new elements must be verified.

facts.title: No Use Outside the Lab
facts.text: Copernicium has no commercial, industrial, medical, or biological role, and it plays no part in any living organism. Its only value is scientific: each atom helps physicists and chemists understand nuclear structure and how relativity reshapes the chemistry of the heaviest elements. In that sense, copernicium is a pure research element, made solely to expand human knowledge.
